name: Magna Carta
info: A royal charter of rights sealed by King John of England at Runnymede in 1215 to make peace with rebel barons; reissued many times, it later became a symbol of liberty and the rule of law.

facts.made: Drafted under the mediation of Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, from the rebel barons' Articles of the Barons; sealed by King John; reissued by the regency of Henry III in 1216 and 1217, by Henry in 1225 and by Edward I in 1297
facts.form: A charter in heavily abbreviated medieval Latin on sheepskin parchment about 15 by 20 inches, sealed with the royal great seal in beeswax and resin; not divided into clauses until William Blackstone numbered them in 1759
facts.where: Four 1215 exemplifications: two at the British Library, one at Salisbury Cathedral and Lincoln Cathedral's on loan to Lincoln Castle; later issues at Durham, the Bodleian, Hereford, The National Archives, Canberra and Washington
facts.known: Runnymede, 1215; clause 61 and the council of 25 barons; clauses 39 and 40 on lawful judgement; annulment by Pope Innocent III; Coke's use against the divine right of kings; influence on the United States Constitution; three clauses still in force in England and Wales

t: The 1215 charter failed as a peace treaty within months, but its reissues from 1216 onwards embedded it in English political life.
From the late 16th century lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke read it as the restoration of an ancient English constitution, an account modern historians call a myth.
The charter concerned the relations between the king and the barons, yet it shaped ideas of due process and influenced the founders of the United States.
dyk: Only three clauses of Magna Carta remain on the statute book of England and Wales: the freedom of the English Church, the ancient liberties of the City of London and the right to due legal process.
ev: King John met the rebel barons at Runnymede, and copies of the agreed charter were issued
Pope Innocent III declared the charter null and void, and the First Barons' War broke out
A reissued charter, with the Charter of the Forest, followed the Treaty of Lambeth and took the name Magna Carta
Henry III reissued the charter of his own free will in exchange for a tax
Edward I reissued it, the version that remains on the statute book
The Petition of Right, supported by Sir Edward Coke, cited Magna Carta in its preamble
William Blackstone published a critical edition and the clause numbers still used
The Statute Law (Repeals) Act left only clauses 1, 9 and 29 of the 1297 statute in force

sections.origins:
England in 1215 was ruled by King John, the third of the Angevin kings, who like his predecessors governed by vis et voluntas, "force and will". Many writers held that kings should rule by custom and law with the counsel of the leading men of the realm, but there was no model for what should happen if a king refused. John lost most of his lands in France to Philip II in 1204, taxed the barons heavily to win them back, and after the defeat of his allies at Bouvines in 1214 returned to find rebels organising in the north and east.

The rebels swore to "stand fast for the liberty of the church and the realm" and demanded that John confirm Henry I's Charter of Liberties. During talks in the spring of 1215 they produced the so-called Unknown Charter of Liberties, which drew on Henry I's charter. John declared himself a papal vassal in 1213, took a crusader's oath and appealed to Pope Innocent III, while the rebels renounced their ties to him and took London. Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, who had worked with the barons on their demands, was asked to organise peace talks.
sections.content:
As David Carpenter noted, the charter "wasted no time on political theory", but it went beyond individual complaints to propose wider reform. It promised the protection of church rights, protection from illegal imprisonment, access to swift justice and, above all, limits on taxation and other feudal payments, some requiring baronial consent. Clauses 2 and 3 fixed reliefs on inheritance, clauses 12 and 14 dealt with scutage, clauses 39 and 40 demanded due process, and clauses on the royal forests promised to reverse John's extensions. Clauses 10 and 11 concerned debts to Jewish moneylenders, and clause 33 ordered fishing weirs removed from rivers.

The charter focused on the rights of free men, in particular the barons, with serfs mentioned in three articles. It was the first document to set English and Welsh law side by side. Under what historians call clause 61, the security clause, a council of 25 barons could seize the king's castles and lands if he failed to correct a breach within 40 days. The historian Wilfred Warren argued that this "was crude in its methods and disturbing in its implications" and almost bound to lead to civil war.
sections.making:
John met the rebel leaders at Runnymede, a water-meadow on the Thames between Windsor Castle and the rebel base at Staines, on 10 June 1215. The barons presented the Articles of the Barons, and Langton's mediation over the next ten days turned them into a charter. By 15 June a text was agreed; on 19 June the rebels renewed their oaths and copies were issued. At least thirteen were made by the royal chancery that year and sent to sheriffs and bishops; there was probably no single master copy. The barons present did not attach their own seals, and the charter carried no signatures.

The text was remade several times. The regency of Henry III reissued it in 1216 without clause 61 and the clauses unfavourable to the papacy. After the Treaty of Lambeth in 1217 a great council issued a new version alongside the Charter of the Forest, and scribes called the larger document magna carta libertatum, "the great charter of liberties". In 1225 Henry reissued it in exchange for a tax of £40,000, declaring it given of his own "spontaneous and free will". Edward I reissued it in 1297 with the Confirmatio Cartarum, and in 1300 with the Articuli super Cartas.
sections.reception:
The 1215 charter failed. Neither side trusted the other, and in a letter of 24 August Pope Innocent III declared it "null, and void of all validity for ever"; the First Barons' War followed. Its reissues fared better. Henry III generally acted within its terms, reformers in 1258 cited it in the Provisions of Oxford, and medieval litigants used it against royal officials. Sir Edward Coke counted 32 reconfirmations between the 13th and 15th centuries, possibly as many as 45. In 1354 a statute of Edward III introduced the phrase "due process of law".

From the late 16th century antiquarians argued that it restored ancient English liberties overthrown by the Normans. Coke invoked it against the divine right of kings, and James I and Charles I tried to suppress such discussion. The Levellers and Diggers judged it a limited grant. Whigs placed it at the heart of the Glorious Revolution, and colonists in America believed it guaranteed jury trial and habeas corpus; the Fifth Amendment's phrase on due process derives from it. Victorian scholars such as Maitland, and Edward Jenks in "The Myth of Magna Carta" of 1904, returned it to its baronial context.
sections.survival:
Four of the 1215 exemplifications survive, each slightly different and each considered equally authoritative. Two came to Sir Robert Cotton in the 17th century, one reportedly found in a tailor's shop and the other at Dover Castle; the second was damaged in the Cotton library fire of 1731 and made largely illegible by a bungled cleaning in the 1830s, but it alone keeps its great seal. Lincoln Cathedral's copy was shown at the 1939 World's Fair and kept at Fort Knox during the Second World War. Salisbury's, perhaps the best preserved, may have been written by cathedral staff.

Later issues survive in Durham, the Bodleian, Hereford, The National Archives and elsewhere. One 1297 copy was bought by the Australian government in 1952; another was sold in 2007 to David Rubenstein for US$21.3 million and lent to the National Archives in Washington. Most clauses were repealed in the 19th and 20th centuries, the first in 1829; since 1970 only clauses 1, 9 and 29 of the 1297 statute remain in force in England and Wales. UNESCO added the four 1215 copies to its Memory of the World register in 2009.
sections.legacy:
Many later constitutions trace their lineage to Magna Carta. Its influence is seen in the laws of Australia, New Zealand and Canada, and clause 29 of the 1297 version remains in force in New Zealand and several Australian states. In the United States it is honoured as an antecedent of the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, and the American Bar Association erected a memorial at Runnymede in 1957. Lord Denning called it in 1956 "the greatest constitutional document of all times".

Most historians now regard its reading as an early charter of universal rights as a myth created centuries later, and Natalie Fryde called it "one of the holiest of cows in English medieval history". W. L. Warren observed that many who knew little of its content invoked its name, "for it meant more than it said". It is generally treated as part of the uncodified constitution of the United Kingdom and is still cited by politicians and campaigners. Its 800th anniversary in 2015 brought the four 1215 copies together at the British Library and a ceremony at Runnymede, and Cornelia Parker's Magna Carta (An Embroidery) was shown at the British Library.

summary: Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215 as a peace agreement with rebel barons and was annulled within months. Reissued by his successors and confirmed as statute in 1297, it was later read as a charter of ancient liberties, a reading historians reject, yet it remains a lasting symbol of the rule of law in Britain and the United States.
